utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make a short statement? Following the testimony of one of the witnesses last week, the witness before last, I believe, we did another search of our files and found what looks like a statement that had not been disclosed to the Defence, which we very much regret. Apparently this statement, if it, in fact, is a statement, was, for some reason, not entered into the computer system and so it was not found. We do not even know if it is a statement. It may be notes of an investigator that was never signed by the witness. But in any event, we propose to turn that over now in its entirety. We have alerted the Victims and Witnesses Unit not to take this witness back until we hear from the Defence as to whether or not they would propose to want to ask her additional questions. Again, I very much regret the late discovery in this and can only say that it was something we just did not know we had until we looked again this weekend. So at this time, I would ask the usher to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This relates to Witness FF or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Witness EE, Your Honour. I might add that we have placed a phone call in to the investigator whose name appears at the front of this statement or notes to determine whether, in fact, it was a signed statement or simply an investigative canvass sheet of some sort, so we should be hearing from that investigator sometime this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, if I may, I should like to raise a matter of procedure regarding the Court order that the Defence is duty-bound to submit its legal view on the criminal responsibility to the Prosecution within a particular period of time. We should like to have the answer to this question, but we also wish to address this matter in a different manner also; that is, we intended that, at the time when we produce evidence, to invite an expert, that is, the President of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina or another person of similar competence and similar responsibility, to explain before this Court concrete valid sentence confirmed by the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina which deals with a crime -- with a war crime which is defined as the persecution of a civilian population of a different religion, that is, Bosniaks, Muslims. We believe that that would give us a more complete picture as to how the question of persecution is addressed by the State whose citizens are accused here. We believe it is very important, that it is very relevant when it comes to Count 1 of the indictment. Therefore, I should like to hear from Your Honours an instruction whether we shall be able to adduce this evidence in the matter as we conceived it, that is, at the time when we produce evidence and bring in our witnesses or would you have another view on the matter? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Krajina. Yes, we believe that you are fully entitled to call this expert as an expert witness when it comes to the Defence case, so as one of your witnesses, an expert witness. Of course, we could stick to our Rules on the expert witnesses. You may ask him to produce a written statement. If there is no challenge, no objection by the Prosecution, we could simply take into account the written statement by the expert witness. However, if you insist that he should be examined and cross-examined, that's even better. I think, in any case, it would be important to have the contribution of the President of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We thought that even this valid sentence could be shown to the Court to try to explain why the sentence was passed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So this judgement will be translated into English, I understand. It could be circulated even before you call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Excellent. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I should like to inform Your Honours about a matter, rather, a problem, which of late has been of considerable concern to both counsel and the accused. I don't know if this is the right time to talk about it, as last Friday afternoon you announced a Status Conference; however, we fear that it might be too late if we waited for that particular session. If I may, I should like to say a few things which concern the time the Defence will need for preparation and adduction of its evidence because this week the Prosecution will exhaust its list of witnesses, at least that is how it was announced, and I'm saying this because come Friday, perhaps you will have some views on this and yet we are afraid that it might be too late to discuss it then because it is very important for the Defence. Your Honour, on several occasions, when considering the necessary time and, of course, bearing in mind your programme or, rather, your timetable for this case, you spoke about four weeks which the Defence would have at its disposal to prepare and call its witnesses and produce the evidence for the Defence. We analysed very carefully all of the commitments before us, and in particular with regard to the preparation of our witnesses, and following that, we arrived at the conclusion that that particular segment of time would not be sufficient for the Defence. In other words, when the Prosecution concludes with the examination of their witnesses, and I think that now already we are faced with some deviations from the statements of these witnesses as against their written statements that were disclosed, these are some quite new facts, some quite new circumstances, and the witness list which the Defence had prepared before this trial began needs to be redefined; in other words, we shall have to -- I wouldn't like to use the word "adjust" the existing, that is, the witnesses we already had in mind in view of the newly arising circumstances but we shall also have to think about calling new witnesses. The difficulties involved -- I presume you could also glean from this part when the Prosecution brought their witnesses, the difficulties in bringing the witnesses here and having their statements are quite obvious. The Defence also has very many difficulties when it comes to the preparation of these witnesses for the Defence and we are planning to call some 80 witnesses. These witnesses are not available to us at all times, and there are some difficulties related to this because some of the witnesses do not really -- or, rather, do not work in their places of residence so that they also go back for weekends, and weekends are the only time when the Defence can establish contact with them and talk to them. However, the most important thing, Your Honours, which I wish to point out and which is a completely new thing, a new situation with which the Defence is faced: Some two weeks ago, or perhaps even more, the proceedings began before this Court in the Blaskic case. It is a fact that one of the counts of the indictment in this particular case is also the one which relates to Ahmici. In other words, the same event which is the subject of hearing before this Chamber. In this particular case, the Defence, in view of the client -- Defence position could not know what the Defence would -- what kind of evidence would the Defence in the Blaskic case adduce, what witnesses they would call, what kind of documents, what kind of papers they would be producing as evidence, and we learned that only when the Defence began its case, so only in the case of the Ahmici event we also learned that several hundred, reportedly 250 different documents, papers, orders, reports are being prepared which are supposed to shed light on every fact related to the events in Ahmici. As this is the same event, perhaps it would be wrong to establish before this Court a different factual situation from the one in the Blaskic case. I do not think it will be good. So in this case, the Defence intends to go through all that documentation, to analyse it, study it, and make an adequate selection, and all of this, Your Honours, takes time. We therefore believe that, along with the preparation of witnesses, we simply cannot do within three or four weeks, that is, a month's time. There is no doubt that the Defence highly appreciates all the efforts that Your Lordships have made to ensure and fair and expeditious trial; however, likewise the Defence is worried what will happen if it does not have enough time for preparation. It is afraid it might miss some relevant facts and that the facts might not be established fully and completely which is, as we, I believe, all agree, a fundamental prerequisite for a fair trial. Your Lordships, in conclusion, I should like to point out that what I am talking about now is the view of all the accused and their counsel. The accused Vlatko Kupreskic and his counsel, of course, if the Chamber goes along with our proposal, will not be against it nor cause any problems. The Defence therefore proposes that in addition to that one month as envisaged by you, we should also be allotted, for all of this business that I mentioned and a number of other things, get another month, that is, not less than two months after the completion of the proceedings which concern the evidence for the Prosecution, that is, all of the witnesses for the Prosecution. Thank you very much, Your Lordships, for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend said a few things about our attitude, and I should also like to add an explanation. We are asking for an extension for the simple reason that we do not intend to refer to documents that were already mentioned and which are used in the Blaskic case, and therefore, we do not think that it is necessary to ask for an extension because we shall not be referring to these documents. But, of course, if Your Lordships go along with what my learned friend has asked for for that extension, we, of course, will go along with that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps when we explain the reasons why we need two months for the preparation of the Defence, perhaps another reason for this is the fact that during the Blaskic case, the unit which attacked Ahmici was mentioned as in this particular case. The event in Ahmici is not disputable, I mean, as the Prosecution described it, but it is disputable when it comes to these accused in the case of Ahmici. The documents which are now produced in the Blaskic case explain how it came about and what units participated in the event in Ahmici, and we think it is very important because so far, in our view, it is still not clear which were the HVO units which attacked Ahmici; and for this reason, we believe that the evidence which is adduced in the Blaskic case, and this is mostly written evidence, that is, objective evidence, not witness statements which, of course, may be suggestive or false and indicate some wrong roads or wrong identification, these are documents which are indicating specific individuals or specific units which participated in it, and the accused here, most of the accused or all -- none of the accused were members of these units, nor did they take part in this action as you will hear from the Defence when we begin our case. Thank you very much. I simply wanted to add this explanation to what my learned friend Pavkovic has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I will turn to the Prosecution to ask about their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand perfectly well what the concerns of the Defence are. I understand that some very useful pieces of information can and must be taken from the proceedings against General Blaskic, but I am concerned in respect of the possible delay that will be brought about thereby. If this Court was to grant the request by the Defence, that would mean, since we are to conclude our case this week, this would mean that we couldn't start until the 15th of December with the Defence case. I don't think that we could use that time for the later part of December, we would have to start in January. Two months will be necessary to hear 70 or 80 witnesses. In other words, we won't be able to conclude this case until late February or the beginning of March with the Defence case, which would be a considerable delay. So we would not have the sentence at this level until May. But I leave it up to you, to your appreciation. I am attached as much as the Court and the Defence is to the fairness of this trial. It is a very complex trial. I understand that evidence must be adduced by the Defence following the Prosecution case, which is no easy task for the Defence, so I leave it up to you to appreciate this whilst we express our concerns. There should not be any problem in ensuring fairness, equality of arms, between the two parties. You know that the difficulties which the Defence is encountering now were the same for the Prosecution when it had to prepare its case. I leave it up to you to assess all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, we are going to think it over. We are going into look into this very sensitive issue. But I am very grateful to Mr. Pavkovic for insisting on the very crucial problem right now. This gives us more time for consideration and possible conclusion as soon as Friday. But if we can, now that we know that we are going to have some 80 witnesses for the Defence - and I agree with you, Mr. Terrier, you may need some two months of hearing to hear all the witnesses - so we have some basic factors to base our decision, our ruling on by Friday, by the time we have our Status Conference. So this being said, in respect of the document we received this morning, I believe that Mr. Radovic, and rightly so, is asking for some time. I suggest we come back to this issue at 2.00 this afternoon to see what the position of the Defence is with regard to this document, to see whether the Defence would like the witness to be called back to expand on her testimony or on his testimony. Before moving on to the next witness, I would like to ask both parties, especially so to the Prosecution, whether it intends to call this anthropologist, Mrs. Bringa. It would be of utmost relevance. I don't know whether the Defence was able to read the book written by the anthropologist and was able to view the film. Could the Defence tell us whether they can agree to this document being tendered into evidence without having the witness coming to the courtroom? We are interested in this witness, and we could call her at the time of the Defence case as a Court witness. This being said, I wonder whether the Defence has made up their minds as to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence has not received the book, nor have we had the opportunity to view the film, because we have not been given it. Therefore, we cannot give your our view on this matter because we are in the dark. However, we do have some views in principle shared by the Defence. We would like to see the expert witness here in the Court, and we would like to be given the opportunity to ask some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's quite sensible that it would be quite visible to call this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We were not able to disclose the book and the film in time. It is quite a major book, a large book, not only in regard of the topic but also in number of pages, and we'd like to disclose the relevant chapters to the Defence, I mean, the chapters which are relevant in view of our case. The chapters that could be interesting for the testimony of the witness. We do, like the Defence and like the Court, wish to call this witness so that she can be questioned by the parties and by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, do disclose the relevant pages to both the Court and the Defence, and do produce the film, and we can already decide that we're going to call this witness as a Court witness -- sorry, yes, Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if in these proceedings we were to use the book written by the lady, then I think that the Prosecutor cannot pick and choose the pages it intends to. If they want to use it as evidence, they need to give us the whole book and then we will see whether the parts chosen by the Prosecutor are really the parts that are relevant, or maybe there are some other chapters in the book which are equally as relevant, seen in the eyes of the Defence. It's not possible for the Prosecutor to tell us what's important for this case and what's not important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We agree. Thank you. We agree. You are right. I think the Prosecutor should be so kind as to produce the whole book. I think that's a very good point. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have one question regarding one witness. Since the examination of the Prosecution witnesses is to be concluded this week, I would like to know why a witness is not on the list for the 9th of October this year. On the list of 30th of the September, we have a witness listed under number 6, and for the list of the 5th of October we have the same witness listed under number 7. On Friday we were informed by the Prosecutor that the witness is here in The Hague, and I would like the Prosecutor to explain what is going on and whether this witness will be examined in the courtroom or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we have the same witness in mind. Indeed, that witness was scheduled on our list of last week, but then we had a fresh look at the counts and the Prosecution evidence, and we do not intend to call this witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. This was to be number 7 on the list of the 5th of October; is that right? She was a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You're not intending to call her?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, this is a highly contentious issues as far as I'm concerned, because I deem this witness to be very important for the case if the facts are to be established correctly. Since this witness is already in The Hague, and since expenses have already been incurred, and in order to prevent her possible return at a later date, I propose that the Court call this witness as a Court witness, since she's already in The Hague. I have another question for the Prosecutor as well. Does the Prosecutor deem that its list of witnesses has been exhausted? Because we do have some witnesses that we would like to propose -- that we would like to be called as Court witnesses to be called by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: As for the last question, you're asking whether this is the final list of the Prosecution witnesses. I assume so. The eight names are there. So if there are other witness, they can be called by the Defence later on when we come to the Defence case. We can't abuse this procedure which we have actually invented, of the Court witnesses, because we are stretching a little bit our Rules of Procedure for the purpose of having a fair trial, and the purpose of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but at the beginning the Prosecutor listed some other witnesses also as Prosecution witnesses, and that was the reason why I wanted to propose that these witnesses be called by the Court, because they're not accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you thinking, in addition to the lady we mentioned before, are you thinking of other witnesses who are on the list, on the previous list and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I don't mean the previous list, but I mean the Prosecution list of 72 witnesses which they said they would call to testify. As far as the lady witness is concerned, I did not state my view on that because we have not been able to examine this part of her statement, the document that we received today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, I think we can't oblige the Prosecution to call the witnesses selected by the Defence. It is a basic right of the Prosecution to call the witnesses they choose to call. I'm sorry. You can call those people as witnesses, Defence witnesses, and, of course, it is our duty as a Tribunal to make sure they come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President today, for me, this witness, who is already in The Hague, is important for me, and I would like to propose that the Court call her as a witness, because otherwise, a significant financial expenses would be incurred, and I think that it is important for this witness to appear before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will decide on this matter in due course. First of all, let me ask the Prosecution about their position on the possible calling of this witness. This witness, I understand, is still here in The Hague, the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In respect of this lady, yes, she is still in The Hague today, and as you mentioned, I do not think the Defence can force the Prosecution to call witnesses the Defence may want to call. We do not intend to call this witness for reasons we need not explain here in detail. If this witness happens to be useful for the Defence, then it is up to the Defence to call that witness as a Defence witness in due course, but we do not intend to call her because we do not think that she's useful for the Prosecution case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will discuss, at the coffee break, this matter in depth, and then we'll come back and make a ruling on this particular witness, whether or not we're going to grant the motion -- or a motion made by Counsel Susak. I think it is now high time to move on to our witness, who has to be cross-examined, I think, by the Defence, and I wonder who -- Counsel Pavkovic, you may be so kind as to tell us who is going to cross-examine this witness, who is witness 1 on today's list.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Counsel Susak intends to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: With regard to that statement that was turned over today, we have just received word from the investigator that, in fact, the statement was never signed, it was never read back to the witness and should be considered not a statement but investigative notes or a -- it was not a statement signed or read back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to this matter later on, maybe early afternoon. All right. Good morning, witness. You will be cross-examined by Counsel Susak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Susak, not too fast so that we can have a good record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Susak:

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will try to do so. I will be very brief. I would like the usher to show to the witness the Exhibit 247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We are in open session. Do you need to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No, it is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what is this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: You mean the photograph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, this aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: This is the building, the warehouse of the construction material, and you can see some other buildings here, some other houses. There is my house here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where is the guard's booth here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: Here, right here (indicating). This is where the door was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where are the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: This is one window, and there was another window on the other side (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: The door is here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please indicate with a pen the location of the doors and the windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: How am I supposed to do so?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you can mark with the pen where the door is, and then you can also indicate with a circle where the windows are.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: The window is here in the back (marks).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark with an arrow the location of the window which is in the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: (Marks).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were two guards on duty or only one when this building was guarded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: There were two of them, but they were taking shifts. I don't know whether the shifts lasted two days or one day, and then -- I know that there were two guards and they were working in shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they on guard duty during the night and during the day as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: No, only in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they working full capacity or what was the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: I think that they were not working full capacity. Believe me, I did not have any insight into their operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But after -- in fact, for how long has this building -- had this building been in operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS GG (continued)
utterances.text: I don't know, believe me. I think it wasn't a recent thing, but I really can't give you an idea as to how long it had already been working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I would like to tender this into evidence, this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe the photograph already is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, as a Prosecution Exhibit, but this is now the photograph with the markings by the witness, so it's a different, in a way, piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This photograph will be marked D7/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honour, I am a little confused. Because this is essentially 247 as a Prosecution Exhibit, P247. It's now been transformed into a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I thought we could have a copy. Could you produce a different copy which would be the Prosecution exhibit--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: -- without any marking, and the one with the marking would be a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have a similar photograph in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I believe we do, or we'll simply make one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So I see there are no questions from the Court. Witness GG, thank you very much indeed for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You intend to call witness number 2; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This witness did not ask any protective measures. This person can be called by his or her name. It will be Sulejman Kavazovic, and we can be in open session. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. To begin with, could you tell the Court what your first and last names are, where you were born and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, good morning. My name is Sulejman Kavazovic. I was born on the 15th of July, 1967, in the municipality of Vitez, in the village of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation in 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 I was a member of the Territorial Defence headquarters in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you specify what your functions were? In that capacity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: From May 1992 until July 1992 I was a military policeman in the Territorial Defence and from July 1992 until 1993 I was the chief for traffic and transport at the Territorial Defence headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you used to live then?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the accused named Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked not to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: -- Court at what time, when, and under which circumstances you got to know Vladimir Santic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in July 1992 I was arrested by the Croatian Defence Council. I was brought to the Hotel Vitez, and I was questioned there by Vlado Santic and two other police officers. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the topic of that interview?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was questioned about the intentions of the Territorial Defence headquarters and why the Territorial Defence was there at all. That was the general gist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him again at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him again on the 24th of April, 1993, when the conflict between the army and the HVO broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your personal situation then on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was a captive, a prisoner. I was taken from one frontline to another, digging trenches, and thus I was brought to the Bungalow where I saw Mr. Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you taken to the Bungalow on the 24th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why I was taken there. I know that I was in the camp in Vitez, in the SDK building where two civilian police officers and a military police officer took me to dig trenches. I spent an hour or two at that location, and after that those same people came and took us in a van to the Bungalow. Probably they needed us to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how Vlado Santic was dressed when you saw him in the Bungalow on the 24th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, on the 24th of April, I was taken from trench digging at Rijeka to the Bungalow. I came there with eight or nine other people who had also been digging trenches at Rijeka. We came in front of the restaurant which was formerly called the Bungalow, and we were lined up there, me and nine other people. I saw Mr. Vlado Santic there. He was wearing a black uniform. And that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many men were at the Bungalow on that day?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, 50 to 60 people wearing different kinds of uniforms, belonging to different units were there. I saw Military Police, I saw some members of the Joker units, some of the HVO members, civilian police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their uniforms and what weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The uniforms were camouflage and black, and the civilian police officers wore blue uniforms. As far as their arms is concerned, they had Kalashnikov rifles and they also had rifles that we used to call, Argentina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vlado Santic speak to you, and if he did, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He said just one word, "You again," and then he ordered four of the members, two from Jokers and two police officers, to take me to Kratine, to Miroslav Bralo, Cicko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, did you have the feeling that Vlado Santic was a commander, had a commanding situation in relation to the other men at the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did have that impression, since he issued an order to these four men to take me to Bralo, Cicko. That indicates that he was in a position of authority, of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, did you see -- did you meet somebody else you knew at the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I saw a woman. I saw her for two or three seconds. Her name was Zumra Jelaskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet other men you would know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I knew only Mr. Ivica Markovic from the civilian police. He was a colleague of mine. He had brought me to the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look around in this courtroom and to tell us whether you do recognise the person you mentioned. I mean, Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I do recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where that person is sitting in the room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He is sitting right across from me, between the two police officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Could you tell us more exactly where he is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: May I point at him? The gentleman is sitting there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give a physical description of that man?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, sure. Well, he's sitting here. His hair is receding, he has a white shirt, a blue coat with a tie. Greying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Lordship, I do have a few questions for this witness and Mr. Radovic too will have some. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, my name is Petar Pavkovic, I'm a lawyer, and I should like to ask you a few questions with regard to what you have just said. Perhaps I could start by asking you, how many times have you so far, if any, given statements to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: About two times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those interviews, did the investigators ask you to describe Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Why, I can't remember that. What do you mean, "describe him"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you told them things that you knew, probably they also asked you what Vlado Santic looked like.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, they asked me once, and I think I explained it somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then do you remember if, on that occasion -- did you describe a person as you see today in the courtroom and, when asked by the Prosecution, you claimed you found that it was Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, except that he wasn't so gray at that time and had more weight at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vlado Santic ever have black hair?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time and before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he 180 centimetres tall?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly. I really cannot measure them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that is not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am telling you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when I ask you, it means, of course, that it concerns some estimates, approximate.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if, at that time, you recalled some details such as, for instance, that you knew Vlado's telephone number and gave the investigators that telephone number?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in '96, '97 sometime. I remember I had to call Vlado. It had to do with an uncle of mine, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still remember that number today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. Today, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this Vlado Santic, are there any other Vlado Santics? Do you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, this is the only Vlado Santic I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you couldn't really recall the telephone number that you referred to at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. By no means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time, when you called Vlado Santic by that number, then you talked to him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know whether this will have any evidential value, but I should like you to bear this in mind when you assess this particular fact. I should like to place at your disposal a certificate of the Vitez post office which shows that the telephone number which this witness stated was indeed Vlado Santic's telephone number but not this Vlado Santic which the witness indicated today but of Vlado Santic, son of Jozo, from Dubravica; and alongside the certificate of the relevant post office, on the telephone number, it's all been translated into English, and I should like to submit it also and to also enclose with it work orders which show that Vladimir Santic, son of Jozo, had asked for a telephone line and that it was provided him on the basis of relevant work orders. So that when the witness said that he talked to Vlado Santic on that particular occasion, it therefore arises that it could be only this particular Vlado Santic, son of Jozo, and not the accused Vlado Santic. So will the usher please take over these documents?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, let us go back to what you said today, that you spoke with Vlado Santic for the first time sometime in September 1992 and that, at that time, you were taken into custody at the Hotel Vitez where you were then interrogated by him and two more men. Could you tell me how positive can you be that Vlado Santic was a member of the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of my interrogation, I was interrogated by Vlado Santic, so he must have been with the HVO. He couldn't be anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it so? Not everybody was in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. I mean, those who did not wear uniforms, who were not in uniforms, they were not either HVO or the TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Vlado Santic do before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was a civilian policeman, member of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time, was he a civilian policeman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a civilian policeman at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Because in Vitez, the civilian police wore blue uniforms and blue caps, and at that time, Vlado Santic did not wear a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if the civilian police was involved, involved in something, wouldn't they have the civilian clothes, as you say, that is, the police clothes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Civilian policemen wore a policeman's blue uniform, sir, throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw Vlado Santic again on the 24th of April, '93, by the Bungalow, and that at that time, you established that he had black clothes on him.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: So he did. On the 24th of April, '93, he was wearing a black uniform, the uniform that was normally worn by the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you assuming that about the Jokers uniform and so --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was not far, a metre or perhaps two metres away from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We were aligned -- they lined up there. We did not talk. He was in the Bungalow and then a soldier called him to come out of the Bungalow, so he came out, and they lined us up on the terrace in front of the Bungalow. There was this terrace. And then he said "You again." And I kept silent because I had not tried to speak. Then he ordered four men, that is two policemen and two Jokers, who were all -- who had -- their heads are shaved except that they had a very small strip of hair here, and he ordered them, "Take them to Kratine."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were nine men. Could you give us some names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Edin Zlotrg, Jasmin Cengalovic, Adnan Pilic, three, I was four, Mirsad Ahmic fifth, Samir Pasagic six, and the other two, I knew their nicknames, one was called Dzampo, and another one, I can't remember it now. I don't know the name and the surname of the last two, but we all came from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had a feeling that Vlado was in command there, of course, when asked by the Prosecution. Why did you have such a feeling?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I had this feeling because when we came out on the terrace, one of them asked Vlado to come out because he said, "Here is the digging team. Will you come out?" And he came out of the Bungalow and he ordered that other foursome to take us to Kratine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any one of that foursome who were ordered?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them. I know that the driver was called Madzar, he was a military policeman, I don't know his name, but he was the one who always drove to Rijeka and back. I know they called him Madzar, and he had those gloves with fingers cut off as a bicycle driver. There was Ivica Markovic, who was a civilian policeman and who drove me there together with them, but he didn't go to Kratine together with us, he went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is only on the basis of that one particular event in which you took part you concluded that Vlado played a part there also?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not a part, an important part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, you are talking about a big role, a small role, but that is not up to you to assess. What I'm asking you is on the basis of what did you assess that? You said you had a feeling.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, because orders came from him. I think that when somebody issues orders, then he must be responsible for things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were with the Territorial Defence headquarters so you also had some military experience, and then I hope you do distinguish orders and what kind of orders.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand something about that because I've been a soldier for the past eleven, perhaps twelve years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time before the conflict, that is, the 15th of April, '93, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In the old part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Vlatko Males mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Males? Yes, of course it does. Vlatko Males was a military policeman, a member of the Territorial Defence, a former active JNA officer. My colleague, shall we say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say something else, something more? Did you see him on that particular day, the 15th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Vlatko Males? No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I saw Mirko Males, his brother. I was accommodated in -- right next to -- with the in-laws and there was Mirko Males also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, '93, did you have any arms?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was a member of the home guards of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, who was a member?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were the head for the traffic of the Territorial Defence. Was there anyone else with you at the headquarters occupying some other posts? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There was the commander of the staff and there was his deputy for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Hakija Cengic was the commander of the municipal headquarters. There was deputy commander for logistics, Muhamed Patkovic, and there were some others but they are not relevant. Should I tell them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There was the commander of the Military Police, Zlatko Nakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was under you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you mean you were on the staff of the --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the staff exist by itself or did you have any units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We had 34 policemen in the staff. There was Anto Furundzija, Vlatko Males.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I am talking about the 15th of April, '93.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, some ten or fifteen military policemen stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not apart from them. That's the lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know -- I mean, does this name mean anything to you, Abdulah Ahmic, called Sudzuka?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Sudzuka? Yes, I know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mustafa, excuse me. Mustafa Ahmic, called Sudzuka?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, during the first conflict on the 20th of October, '92, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All day?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I started that day from Visoko to Vitez to report to the Territorial Defence command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went through Ahmici. The conflict was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Mustafa Ahmic, called Sudzuka, at the Territorial Defence headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was at home, in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was he? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was at home, in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did he have any kind of communication with the Territorial Defence headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, sometimes perhaps, but I don't know what you mean. He had no responsibilities. He was not in command. He had nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time, in Ahmici, was there a radio station of a kind?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you that in answering the investigators, you told them that this Ahmic was in Ahmici, that he had his radio station, and that he called you to ask for help.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. He called. He didn't ask it from me because I was responsible for traffic. He couldn't get me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean the staff.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He said -- yes, he called the Territorial Defence. He said, "My house is on fire. I need help." Something like that. But I could not help him and he did not ask for this help from me specifically. He was asking the Territorial Defence, the commander, to help him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where were you on the 16th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you mentioning the month of April because I'm not quite sure with the Croatian language. I know in Bosnian it is April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand you. I understood you when you were speaking Bosnian and yet I'm not protesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I shall try to speak so that you will understand my Bosnian. So will you please tell me, where were you on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was at my in-laws' place in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 18th of April, '93. I was under a sort of house arrest because I could not move around, I could not go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that house arrest, it was the time of war, so you placed yourself under arrest because -- I mean, you were in. Nobody put you there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They kept the buildings closed. Muslims were not allowed to move about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were in a flat?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the flat. I mean, no, we were not allowed to go into the street whenever we liked, so that there was a kind of arrest. There was the HVO, the Territorial Defence were around -- around the buildings, and those who came out, they took us to camps, and that is what happened to me on the 18th of April. A man came who took me away and all the men from the building, they took us to the building of the social auditing service, and that is where we were put under custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Bungalow, you said that when there, you saw an individual -- I'm afraid I did not note the name of that person -- it was Zumra something?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw two women. I didn't know the second woman, but Zumra, as we were standing on the terrace -- I'm explaining how I saw those two women. We were lined up there, and I was the last one -- or, rather, the first on the left side, and when we were lined up, that soldier, he told us to stand one beside the other and we did, and for a second, I turned my head to the left, and behind the corner of that Bungalow restaurant, those two women turned up, and I just cast a look. But the soldier who was sitting across from us -- there were not many of them, but one of them said, "You two, back -- back off." So I turned, I saw this Zumra Jelaskovic, whom I knew from Vitez. She was the wife of an instructor from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it important to mention them? because you must have seen very many other things and people.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, perhaps. But to me, those women -- those women were not supposed to be there, I guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us leave aside what you guess. You say that you think there were about 50, 60 people there, and you said that military and civilian police, HVO -- where were all those people? Did you count them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not count them. I said approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were they lined up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were sitting, sitting down. They were in uniforms, they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they sitting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: They were sitting in the parking lot of that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In one place?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, in a circle. There were about 50 or 60 -- I did not count them, really -- but about 50 or 60, three types of uniforms, camouflage, black, and blue, of the civilian police. They were sitting there chatting. And after a while -- I really don't know what they were doing there, but there were that many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did you see Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the whole period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean on that particular occasion.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, only then, for about a minute, minute and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Your Lordships, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have more questions, and I intend to be quite exhaustive about the Territorial Defence and the like. Perhaps it would be an appropriate time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Before we take a break, I wonder whether Mr. Moskowitz could be so kind as to indicate to us the date of the interview on that document which was distributed before, because now it's only the 31st of July, 1st of August. There is no year. The Defence counsel may wish to know the full date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. The information we have from the investigators was 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 1996. All right. Thank you. We will now adjourn for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Since the witness is not here, I'll read out the ruling we have made in the case raised this morning by Counsel Susak. The Court considers that the Prosecution is fully entitled to decide, for reasons that it does not need to explain to the Defence and the Court, not to call a witness previously listed as a Prosecution witness. Whenever the Prosecution takes such a decision, if the Defence intends to call the witness, it may do so at a later stage, in the course of the Defence case. The witness would then be called as a Defence witness. In that event, the Court will assure that he or she is brought to The Hague to testify. However, in this instance, the Court considers that it is faced with exceptional circumstances that warrant a departure from the aforementioned principle. The witness is currently in The Hague, having been brought here by the Prosecution as a prospective witness. It might prove difficult or inexpedient to recall her to testify at a later stage. In addition, this witness might provide exculpatory evidence. The Court, therefore, holds that it is in the interests of fairness and justice to call the witness now, in the course of the Prosecution case. On the strength of Rule 54, the Court does decide to call the witness as a Court witness, and instructs the Victim and Witnesses Unit to bring the witness to court this afternoon. She will be briefly examined by the Court, then cross-examined by the Prosecution and re-examined by the Defence. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic. Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, at the Territorial Defence staff in Vitez, you were in charge -- there was also the security sector?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That's very likely, but I was in charge of the transport and traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a person in charge of traffic and transport, you were a chief. Did you have meetings of all the chiefs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At those meetings, did you see a person -- an officer in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was in logistics. There were no security officers in logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is a person in charge of the security in the staff, and the person in charge of security, the security officer, is concerned about everything, including logistics?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I had a colleague -- actually, there was an officer who was above me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not directly subordinate to the commander, to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a person who was between you and the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a person who was in charge between me and the logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that before the 16th, that is on the 15th, the Territorial Defence staff was provided information by the security officer that a great danger was imminent?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the security officer, but you could see that in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. What I'm interested in is whether the Territorial Defence staff, located at the time in Stari Vitez, had been warned that serious danger was imminent?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that due to possible danger, it was decided that members of the Territorial Defence staff should spend the night, from the 15th to the 16th of April, at the staff premises?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I for one did not spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come, if you were a member of the staff, that you were not informed of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I gave you the reason. I was in the logistics staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about this. You said that you have been in the army for quite some time. I assume that you served in the JNA before the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time are you an officer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm an officer of the BH army, and I have the rank of First Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you in charge of? Are you still in the logistics branch?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm at the joint command of the army. I'm in charge of transport and traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the eve of the 16th, do you know whether the Territorial Defence in Stari Vitez and around Stari Vitez ordered some trenches to be dug?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked on the 15th when the Territorial Defence staff was formed. Pero Skopljak and others attended that meeting. They were invited to be there when the Territorial Defence was formed. That was celebrated at the day of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not ask whether that was dug on the 15th of April, I'm just asking whether there were any trenches dug before that in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see any trenches, because I went to the part of the town with the majority of the Croatian population and I would have seen some trenches there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have seen them if you travelled on the road?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But could you see other trenches dug in other places? Are you able to say that on the basis of your own perception?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now tell me, the feast of Bajram on the 19th -- in 1993. It was on the 22nd and 23rd of March, 1993. Do you know where this was celebrated in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was in the camp. I couldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the 22nd and 23rd of March.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know where it was celebrated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not hear that the feast was celebrated in the fire-fighting brigade centre?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not celebrate Bajram in that year?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Sefkija Didic's function in the Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, did not hear the name of the person replacing-- whom he replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic is broaching questions which were in no way raised during examination-in-chief. In the present case, this cannot be motivated by the desire to assess the reliability of the witness. I am perfectly aware of the fact that the Court can grant some questions outside the scope of the examination-in-chief, but if this is justified, if this is the view of the Court, then it means that Mr. Radovic should have less leading questions to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, you heard the objection from the Prosecutor. We are wondering about the relevance of your questions, because he's right there, the Prosecutor is right that you -- in saying that you are going beyond the matters raised in examination-in-chief. Could you point to the relevance of your questions for your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: The question concerning the Bajram in Stari Vitez will form a part of the Defence of the accused. We can say that at this stage, since we are now approaching the end of the Prosecution case, his Defence will be that he was on friendly terms with the Muslims up until the very last minute -- that's the part of the indictment concerning persecution -- and that on the night of the 22nd to the 23rd of March, his folklore group danced Croatian and Muslim folk dances at the party, at the celebration of the feast of Bajram at the fire brigade centre of Stari Vitez. That is in the area controlled by the Muslims. I am asking this question -- in fact, I should ask this question of every Muslim who appears here, since do I not know which of the witnesses attended that celebration of the feast of Bajram and which one was able to see the Kupreskic brothers dance in celebration of Bajram. Because if it is claimed that they are engaged in the persecution of Muslims, then it can only concern the one day, the day of the 16th. But if the indictment covers a longer period, we have to prove what their conduct was throughout that period. The point is it is very hard for us to come into contact with Muslim witnesses, and in my view -- I don't know if you will share this view with me -- you will give greater weight to confirmation of Muslim witnesses if they say what -- in what way the Kupreskic brothers treated them. So that was the reason I asked this question. As far as the Territorial Defence is concerned, he was on the staff of the Territorial Defence and I'm just trying to determine what he knows about the organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we consider that your questions are relevant. You may proceed. Although they go beyond the matters raised in examination-in-chief, they are relevant so you are allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have concluded the matter of Bajram. I have a few more questions about the Territorial Defence. We have already heard about that from other witnesses, but since he has first-hand knowledge, having been in the organisation, maybe he can tell you something about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you join the staff, and whether at that time it was a joint body of Croats and Muslims, or was it separate right from the start?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the Territorial Defence staff on the 22nd of May, 1992. The staff was formed by a joint command, Croat and Muslim in the town of Vitez. It was in the premises of the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to go into such detail. Can you please tell us when the two separated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in August when Anto Furundzija and the other gentleman left the Territorial Defence staff, the other Croatians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did the Territorial Defence staff move to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: When the first conflict broke out on the 21st of October, 1992, when we were surrounded by the HVO, and when the HVO simply evicted us from the buildings because they considered themselves to be the only armed force. They were stronger. There were only about 35 of us. In Vitez there were many units which were the not from the Vitez municipality but from Mostar or from Siroki Brijeg, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us more concrete details?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, the Ludvig Pavlovic unit from Mostar. They had the HVO patches with the laurel leaves. They also captured me on that very day, the 22nd of October, and brought me to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when the Territorial Defence staff moved to Stari Vitez, did the staff have some kind of a base or were there just people? What I mean is did they have any units of which it was in charge?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, it did not have any units. There were about 20 people on the staff. We did not move. We had been evicted. They allowed us to leave through the town centre, but when we started leaving they arrested us. Mr. Vlado Santic should know that, he was present at the time. The commander and three or four other men were allowed to move to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when the staff moved to Stari Vitez, did they have any arms at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was arrested. I spent four days in the Ministry of the Interior, in detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But after that, when you were released, you went to the Territorial Defence staff?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I would like to know whether you had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There were some automatic rifles, 10 or 12 military police officers were there. I did not have that information at my disposal, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the 20th of November, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1992. Apology. I meant the 22nd of October.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the staff, at the headquarters, but I heard about the roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear who ordered the roadblock to be set up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I have no idea. A roadblock was set up by the HVO and another roadblock by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who manned the roadblock, who ordered the roadblock to be set up? You don't know anything?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know anything about the formation of the 325th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Territorial Defence and the brigade, that is two separate matters?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but before the Territorial Defence was set up, the Territorial Defence staff was in charge of the Territorial Defence units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Units? Well, was there an organisation structure of the Territorial Defence on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, I can -- I was in the town. I was not allowed to go around, because I was given orders by the chief for logistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the formation of this Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would have no further questions for this witness. However, in respect of the documents submitted by Mr. Pavkovic earlier on, I do not think that they could be usefully tendered into evidence inasmuch as we do not have -- I don't mean the originals, I'm not asking for the originals, but we do not have copies of the Bosniak or Bosnian versions so as to verify the authenticity or the conformity of the translation into English. On the other hand, these documents, according to me, only prove this: That the son of Jozo, Vlado Santic, had a telephone line, the number of which is given, and that on the 27th of October, 1994, somebody rang him. I do not see how this piece of information is connected to our case and could be in any way useful to the file in this case. So failing any other information from Mr. Pavkovic, we oppose this document being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I was also wondering why we had not been provided with a copy of the original in Bosnian Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not have the original at this time. I don't have it here, but I do have it elsewhere. I can submit the original both to the Chamber and to the Prosecution. In fact, it was by mistake that I don't have this original, because I actually thought that you would be able to understand what this is all about on the basis of the translation.
