I knew that I was looking for an individual who had been seriously burned, and so I was asking people in the hall where I could find this individual. See, I was extremely pressed for time, and I'd already wasted a lot of time by going to the cinema. So I was trying to get to this individual as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe where he was and what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to an orderly or a physician, I'm not sure, a man in a white coat, and asked for this person, and he directed me to a room where I found the individual in question, together with a number of family members, including children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you describe the condition this man was in when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He was lying in bed propped up with a pillow. His -- both hands were bandaged. He was injured on one side of his face quite seriously. For the most part covered with a sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you speak with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your purpose in speaking with him? What were you trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The not really convey. I wanted to tell him -- I did. I wanted to tell him that I found his family, and I wanted to provide the information to British battalion for their burial, and my primary goal was to get their names and to be able to relay that message -- that information back to British battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell this man that you had, in fact, found his family and also the circumstances in which you found them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult -- he was grateful. It was very important, even though he was a witness, that someone had found his family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he provide you the names of the individuals who were in that house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were speaking with him were you jotting down or scribbling down notes on a piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a piece of paper and a pen with me because I wanted to take down their names. And I also asked specific questions like, "Where would he like his family to be buried, and would he like a religious leader present, and if so, who would that be?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he provide you with those names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you have those names with you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not, but I did send a memo to British battalion describing -- with their names, and the name of the Imam that he had requested, and where to bury them. I don't have it with me. I haven't seen it in a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this gentleman -- by the way, did you come to know his name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: This was [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did [redacted] then, after expressing his gratitude, provide you with additional -- or began to speak about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He basically repeated to me what I had been told the day before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your recollection of what he told you that day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that -- that firing had started in the village at an early hour, 5.30, and that they remained in their home. Through the window they could see soldiers going up and down the streets, and could hear firing. He told me that the at one point soldiers were heading in the direction of his home, and that he then tried to hide in different places around the room, and that these individuals entered the room, immediately went to the second room, where he could hear and to a certain extent also see that they had shot his family, and that those individuals then poured petrol around the room, including at a certain point he was behind a couch, also on the couch he was hiding behind or near, and set that ablaze.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you that he either knew or did the not know who was responsible for that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I asked him that question. I asked him -- actually, I'm not even sure if I asked him per se. He had probably mentioned a name, and I said, "So you knew these individuals." And then he indicated to me, "Of course I knew them," something like that, "Of course I know them." Which, of course, there was a reaction from the others in the room as well to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he indicate not by name but by some other way who these people were?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He mentioned, yes, "My neighbours from the first house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you press him to give you a name, or was that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. As I say, I was not interested in perpetrators. The only reason that I even asked that question was -- I wanted to know whether or not to pass on that information to any future investigation, that he would be someone for them to talk to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, pass on the information about the names of his family to BRITBAT?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you were taking some scribbled notes down on a piece of paper while he was speaking to you. Do you know what happened to those notes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point later on did you attempt to reconstruct your conversation with [redacted] and --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Through a little memo of some sort?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Part of this same one. This is days after the report had been submitted and we were hopeful that there would be a full-scale investigation, and so I attempted to put down whatever we had to be able to assist a future investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, do you have that little memo you did on [redacted] in front of you? You might want to take a look.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there names of his family listed there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read them out, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Last names are Nazer Ahmic, Zehrudina Ahmic, Elvis Ahmic and Sead Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour. I have no more questions at this time but would proffer the Exhibit P -- I think it's 286, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, just a moment. Mr. President, perhaps the Defence counsel could have a look at this exhibit. We do not know what is this document that has been tendered into evidence by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We haven't tendered it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: There has been a misunderstanding then. I would like to advise you, Mr. President, that this witness will be examined by the Defence counsel Ranko Radovic, Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, Luko Susak, and I also will have two questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when you had arrived in Ahmici that you looked for sniper positions, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, am I correct that you were able to locate sniper positions by looking for lots of shell casings?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't say that I was looking specifically because of shell casings and so on, I was told that there were a number of bodies collected from a certain area, more than anywhere else, and that the injuries that were reported to me by British battalion were single shots to the head and neck. This led me to believe, as well as many others, there was a group of people that were discussing this, that this was just not -- that this would be direct fire, and the indication was that there could have been snipers operating because of the accuracy of these shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your military education?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I have none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What then leads you to believe that the only accurate shots -- accurate shots could only be fired from a sniper, or to be more precise, from a rifle having the sights, the telescopic sights?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: This came from what was -- my conversation with British battalion officers who have military experience, and in their opinion -- this was brought up by us, but in their opinion it was very possible -- we're not saying that was confirmed, but it was very possible that snipers were operating in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we were not discussing sniper operations at this time, but only that the bodies, the dead bodies that you found had been hit from a sniper rifle or from an ordinary rifle?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I could not understand. If you could repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you came to that conclusion on the basis of your conversations and on the basis of the fact that these people had been shot with a single bullet or two bullets, and that this was -- that it was possible that snipers were operating in that battle area. So now my question is: What facts were used by your informants when they reached the conclusion that the dead bodies were shot by a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we ever drew a conclusion as such. I mentioned that we looked in that area because we had information to believe, but I don't think that we ever concluded anything with regard to snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's much better. Now, tell me, when you're talking about issues having to do with military knowledge, are you giving us your own opinion or the opinions of your informants? And as you already told us, your informants, sources of information, were officers of the British battalion.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not exclusively British battalion. There were a number other people that we had raised questions with, including European Community monitors and other members of UNPROFOR in different locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You obtained information about traces or evidence found in Ahmici, and on the basis of that information certain conclusions were made regarding the kind of weapons from which these people were killed. What kind of knowledge, what kind of information about that could ECMM monitors have? What information did you receive from the European Community monitors? To be more specific, I thought that you had received all your information from the British, because they were officers, military officers, with a certain kind of military experience, and now you're talking about EC monitors. So now tell me, what relevant military information did you receive from the ECMM monitors?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that at any point I claimed to describe the military operation at all. I don't -- I don't see where we described weaponry, other than shell casings or -- I think the only other weapon I mentioned was petrol. Our investigation was not of the military operation per se. I honestly don't believe that I relayed any military facts at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about military operations, I'm asking you about traces, evidence, physical evidence. Shell casings, that's evidence. You claim that you received information about this evidence -- I'm talking about the shell casings and the wounds sustained by the victims -- from the British battalion members. I'm not talking about the military operation. Military operation, that's planning and execution. I'm asking you about the evidence that you found as a monitor employed by Mr. Mazowiecki. On the basis of the traces of evidence that you found, what conclusions did you draw?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The conclusions that there was a -- the conclusions that were drawn, as were put in the report, are that there was a sustained military operation in the village of Ahmici, and that as a result, approximately 180 homes had been destroyed and that a number of people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not draw any conclusions regarding the shell casings found?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: At one point when we were visiting -- when we were visiting the field, we asked. We looked for shell casings just because we had an indication that snipers could be operating in that area, and we asked a simple soldier who was next to us what he thought this would be. We were not looking to even collect evidence. For example, that shell casing was never collected. No other evidence was ever collected in terms of casings or any other military hardware that was left in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you looked for sniper shell casings. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I will go on to my next question. When you looked for the sniper shell casings, according to you, what's the difference between the sniper shell casing and an ordinary rifle shell?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in ballistics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were looking at this, as you just told us. You were looking for sniper rifle shells. So now please tell us what was it you were looking for on the ground in Ahmici? How would you distinguish a sniper rifle shell from an ordinary rifle shell? You, you are not an expert, so I would just like to know how did you spend your time when you were looking for those shells?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The -- looking for sniper positions, looking for sharpshooter positions. I'm not using the term "sniper" in terms of a sniper will have a certain type of weapon, will conduct warfare in a certain way, but sharpshooters are someone that would use his position and weapon to obtain a certain effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I fail to understand. This is your assumption as to what a sniper is. It is very clear what a sniper is. You told us that you had been looking for evidence of sniper rifles being deployed there on the basis of shell casings. Can you now tell me -- this is the third time I'm now asking you this question -- how could you distinguish the sniper rifle shells from ordinary shell casings?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't distinguish them at all. In fact, I never really received a hundred per cent confirmation that snipers were operating. This was just something that -- we were attempting to find firing positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This is really more or less what you could find there. You also spoke about petrol being used to burn houses. Was I correct in my understanding? What physical fact that you found on the ground lead you to believe that petrol was used to burn those houses?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We never investigated the -- as I mentioned earlier, we are not criminal investigators, and we did not conduct a criminal investigation or a forensic investigation of how the homes that had been destroyed, the manner in which they were destroyed. Speaking from just what we saw, it was apparent that the homes had been gutted by flames for the most part from the inside, and the reason I believe that is that many of the external walls were standing, while as the multiple storeys and the roof, which in my understanding the beams are of wood and other flammable materials, would have burned and fallen into itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, are you aware of incendiary bullets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible to set on fire from the inside if you fire an incendiary bullet into the house and it hits a wooden object and then the house burns from the inside?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible to set a house on fire very quickly if you set a curtain on fire with a match, and you don't even have to use petrol in that case?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I would imagine so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In such a case, is it necessary to use petrol? In other words, is it then -- is it a credible conclusion that petrol was used?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, sorry to interrupt you. The witness is not an expert witness. He's not an expert in incendiary weapons, and petrol and so on. I don't see any point in asking these questions. If you're asking for hypothetical answers, all right, but as I say, I don't see any relevance. He's a factual witness. He's a witness of fact. He has no expertise in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I know, but he draws some conclusions about things he does not have an expertise in, about snipers, about manners in which houses were set on fire. I just want to point out the fact that in his notes he's talking about things he doesn't know a lot about. But at any rate I just have one more question and then I'll be drawing to a close.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming to be an expert, but I was told by numerous witness that petrol was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you're reporting a fact?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm reporting a fact, relaying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Not even fact. The opinion of other persons. So he's simply reporting the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this is not his own conclusion on the basis of what he found on the ground, but he's just reporting other people's opinions. I can agree to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, again, I have to ask you this question: Can you give me the names of the people who told you that? Do you have those names noted down --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- or is it possible for you to remember all those names? So you're unable to give us the names of the people who told you that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was waiting for the translation to end. Yes. I can distinctly remember Sakib Ahmic telling me that petrol was used inside of his home. Specifically he told me that. And numerous other people from -- from my encounters in the Zenica cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Of these other people, do you know any names? We know about Sakib Ahmic. We're not challenging the fact that he was telling you about this.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that (redacted) also told me that petrol was used. Those are the two names that I can confirm told me that petrol was used, by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just these two people and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came to Vitez -- or, rather, in Ahmici, you went there with the assistance of the British battalion. Who gave you the first general information about Ahmici before you even went there on the ground?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the officer in charge of briefing at British battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not, but he would be -- I think that that was his full-time function, if I'm not mistaken, to brief officers on the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have no more questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Radovic. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac? I'm sorry, it's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes. After the break, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll take a break now. Sorry, I had not realised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If I may, I shall have some introductory questions, and I should like, if I may, to keep it in closed session for a few introductory questions. It is only for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We are in closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. (closed session)

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: (Open Session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if it was the same person that you gave the dictaphone to record her statement on a tape? Was that one of those persons? You said that there were two persons who recorded their statements on tape.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It is very possible, but I'm not 100 per cent. It is possible. The person that I can see in my head had the basic same build and colour of hair, but I'm not 100 per cent because this particular individual that I handed the tape to, I really had no special conversations with her. She just wanted to speak into the tape recorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What person are we referring to? The one who made a longer statement or the one that made a shorter statement? Are we referring to the latter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the person who made the short statement, not the administrator from the clinic but the other person. I believe her last name is [redacted] and first name is [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how was the exact location of the house described to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was described as a smaller house -- if I recall correctly -- a smaller house in a group of other homes in between the two roads. That was the basic description. And then a house number was given, but I was also told that it's very difficult to find it by just looking for the house number, but to look between the two -- between two roads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the number 5 on the house still there or was the house completely burned down; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw the number on the house. I was told that House number 5 had been found. I actually never saw the number, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Tell us then, you knew what your duty was: You were supposed to answer questions relating to human rights in the Lasva Valley at the time. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We were actually not instructed to conduct any kind of investigation, but in the normal course of our duties as human rights officers, this was something that fell within our mandate. Once we had established some basic facts, we brought it to the attention of certain individuals in Geneva who were there to support Mr. Mazowiecki, that we believed that we should look into this matter and that an investigation or the Special Rapporteur should take interest in this particular area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But then you knew that with regard to those events which you monitored, the state of human rights, violations of human rights, you knew that you would be writing some reports, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everything that we did in terms of fact-finding dealt with the human rights situation, in very broad terms, throughout the former Yugoslavia. The mandate of Mr. Mazowiecki was such to report and provide, if you will, a reference document about the state of human rights throughout the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, during those seven days, you were only involved in that particular narrow area. During those seven days you were not involved, you were not monitoring in any way, human rights in other parts of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: This was a special case. This was a little bit different than a lot of things that we had done previously and after that. There was a call for someone to do something in that area, and we didn't know if we were the ones that could provide that. We certainly weren't qualified to do it. But Mr. Mazowiecki wanted to bring the world's attention, and that was the mechanism in the Centre for Human Rights, to report to the Secretary-General of the United Nations who would then relay that information on to the General Assembly or to the Security Council, that is indeed the mechanism. So our job was to provide information and to hope that governments and other institutions would take action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it was to establish certain facts which you saw there. Now, tell me, you took some notes while talking to witnesses in the cinema; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you equally took notes during interviews with [redacted] at a hospital?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you equally took notes when you talked to those persons in the cinema for the first time, the first time when there were those people from Ahmici, when you singled out people from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also compiled some notes, that is, you took off the videotapes the statements of those two eyewitnesses; you also took notes of that, of those two women who taped their comments, their interviews?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, on each of these occasions, you took notes and you established facts in this way; is that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you turn over those notes to? I mean, in view of their importance, you said it was very important to establish what really had happened there, and you thought that it could serve as grounds for future investigation, you already said it, and you had found some facts and collected them. I should like to know, who did you give them to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't give them to anyone because we had no mechanism. That was one of the frustrating things about the Centre for Human Rights and the mandates of the United Nations at that time. We had no procedure in which to seal, collect, hold, file; there was no body that would deal with that type of information whatsoever. The information and the notes were contained here in what was referred to as an interim report. This report or Mazowiecki's mandate, for the most part, is done with on-site visits, and the individual, or Mr. Mazowiecki in this case, reports to the Economic and Social Council as well as to the Secretary-General. These are the notes. Unfortunately, we had no procedure. It was extremely frustrating. I agree. This is one of the things that was very difficult for all of us in the Centre as well as other organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of this report, and presumably some other reports and television recordings, in '95 the indictment was filed for the same event. Did anyone from the Prosecutor's Office talk to you, turn to you and ask about such notes, about the existence of such notes, because you had been there, you had been there immediately after the events?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked about the notes and I was asked about the tape as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give any of this material to the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Not personally. I did direct, when asked, I did direct them to the Centre for Human Rights' office and told them that there is a possibility that something may remain there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the Office for Human Rights had some notes? Had you turned over a part of your notes or perhaps a tape? I mean the Centre for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't turn anything over. As I said, there was no procedure in which to turn anything over, no body or no procedure. However, I had worked in the office for quite some time, and we had accumulated files that were used for field purposes, and I had hoped that there was some of that information there. I don't know if they actually -- well, I don't know if they went to the field office, but I can tell you that I was provided today with my typewritten notes that I haven't seen and I do not personally have a copy. I was provided with a copy today and I haven't seen that for quite some time, although I do now have a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so it is quite possible that some of these notes stayed behind, I mean, at the Centre for Human Rights; is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, actually, unfortunately, I know that there have been several attempts -- not necessarily even directed at this case but at other cases -- to find notes in the Centre for Human Rights, and as far as I know, very little, if anything, was found. I really don't know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As regards this event, the event related to Sakib Ahmic, the whole event is described with considerable precision, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall quite a bit about my conversation with Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if Sakib Ahmic said that he had seen how his grandchildren were killed; do you remember that? So that he would really affirm with certainty that he knew that his children had been killed before the house was put on fire; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The latter part of your question, the way you formulated it, did he see, the way it was relayed to me, I had the impression that he was able to witness what had happened in the house. Did he actually say, "I saw them being killed"? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I was referring to his knowledge that his children had been killed. Was this something that you learned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In other words -- no, absolutely. When I walked in the room to get information from him, he -- it's interesting, because when I arrived, I think that others in the room were some of the individuals that I had talked to in the cinema. And when I came to the room, he knew who I was. I told him that I had found his family, and he knew that, and I asked him at that point what would he want done with the bodies and where would he like for me to provide, if possible, a burial. He was very clear on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, who were these persons in the hospital at the time when you were there? You said the persons that you talked to in the cinema.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There were -- there were several children --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also the girl that you mentioned, the one that said that she was the mechanic's daughter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I don't believe she was there. I would remember her, and I don't recall her being there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That other person who gave you the report?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. It's very possible. I have to tell you, when I came into that room I was extremely nervous. I was under time constraints, and I had never told anyone, in my life, that I had found his family, and this was very difficult for me to do. I came into a room where there was a man seriously injured who I had to relay this to, and it was very painful for me, and I can imagine even more so for this individual. I tried to do as little talking as possible and let this individual speak to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that the woman who had given you the information about the house was there. That's [redacted]. That's what you said her name was. Was that other person who had given you the initial report, or who had recorded the statement, was she there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I said it was possible that Sedeta was there. It's possible. The reason I say that is because I was immediately welcomed there. He knew exactly who I was, and he also knew exactly what I came to tell him. I mean, I felt that. I felt that. It was just --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell me, do you remember whether that other person was there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. She had a very strong presence. I -- if I said it was possible for Sedeta to be there, I think that it's not probable that the first person was there. I don't believe that she was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to ask you one question. You said that in the three visits to Zenica, to the cinema, to the hospital, you talked exclusively with the family of [redacted] --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- his daughter, his daughter-in-law and his granddaughter. These are the only persons that you remembered from those three visits. Can you recall any other person?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I talked to -- I talked to 30, 40 people. And many of the people that I spoke with -- these are just the names of people that actually had information that was very specific, that I was looking for. Many of the individuals that I talked to had fled early that day, or had escaped by different means and so on and had not actually witnessed crimes. I was looking for witnesses, not just people that were from that village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were looking for witnesses, but it's possible that there were people there who had somebody killed. You gave us information only concerning these three people. Can you tell us about any other person of whom you have some more detailed information regarding the event in Ahmici and that you also had spoken to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to -- let's see. There was a lady that was -- I don't know if she introduced herself, but I remember her as the mechanic's wife, and the reason I remember it as such is when I was asked about what I'd seen in the village, she said, "Did you see a house that had a mechanic's shop?" and so on. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where would that house be? Did she tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't -- I believe that that house was a bit lower in the village, and that's why we didn't visit. If I'm not mistaken. It would be in this area here (indicating), if I'm not mistaken. If I recall, it would be down here somewhere. It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to a car mechanic; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. There were a number of other individuals. There was a group of individuals that were from a different part of Ahmici, if I can call it the upper part of Ahmici. There were -- there was a group of two or three that had been together with the clinic administrator, (redacted) who were also present.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I don’t even know that now. who?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that until today -- until now. I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered the house, who else entered the house with you? You were in the house number 5 on that day when you found her -- found it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I entered possibly third or fourth into house number 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many bodies were found on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I personally saw what I thought were three bodies, and one was very distinct and was also shown on the video. However, in the left-hand corner of the room there were two remains that were not really associated -- they could have been together, they could have been separate, but I believe that there were three remains visible in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to see clearly that these were bodies when we're talking about the two remains, or was it really hard to say that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: One was very clear. The other two remains -- or the other two partial -- because I wasn't really clear if that was one that had been split into two pieces, if you will, or was it one body. However, it was -- I mean, there were things that immediately told you that yes, these are remains, but the other two not very clearly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody who was with you that day there have any kind of forensic experience that would enable that person to tell you exactly what it was, since we could see on the photographs that it wasn't very clear.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I believe that was done once the bodies had been collected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the bodies taken to be autopsied? Do you know anything about that, or to be examined in any way?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have no information of what happened after the bodies were collected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the conversation with [redacted], you said that he had given you names of the perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that he gave me names. He may have, because something led me to ask him, "So you knew these individuals," because I remember asking that question. And his response at that time was, "Of course I know those individuals." But I didn't write down a name or ask him any further questions. That was probably --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he tell you the names? Did he give you the names, even if you didn't note them down?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He may have. Not names, not names. I believe that if he did say something it was a name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall which name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You further stated that these had been neighbours, next-door neighbours. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's how he relayed the information to me. He said -- he --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He referred to it as, "My neighbours."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say -- did he specify neighbours from which house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He said -- he said, "Of course I know. Of course I know these people. It's my neighbours in the first house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but all the Croats live in houses next door to his house. There are three or four houses surrounding his house, so this is not a distinctive feature. Did he give you any specific information? That's the reason why I'm asking you this.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't looking for any house or anything. I was told that it was his neighbours from the first house, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing more specific?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were involved? Did he give you that information?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: The -- I can't be precise on that, but it was definitely -- it was in plural. He was speaking about "soldiers", he was speaking about up and down the road, and then he was speaking about when "They came into my house," which means there's definitely more than one, but I don't recall asking or being told how many individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he talk about soldiers and neighbours or just about soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He -- he talked about the attack on this general area right close to his home in a way that he was hoping that they wouldn't come towards his house, and then -- that they then came to his house, and at that time, that's when he mentioned a name of some kind. And I can't remember. Sort of like, "That's when so and so came into my house." And I wasn't very clear, I couldn't hear the name, but I said, "So you knew these people." And then he said, "Of course, these are my neighbours from the first house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that he observed the movement of those soldiers through his window.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: He observed their movement through a window, or through door or how he observed, but, yes, he told me he observed movement for some time through the window or through the door. He observed movement outside of his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some other family members were there, and probably that one person from the cinema and some children. Was there -- were there any other adults in the hospital with him when you were there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the room?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean in the hospital room.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: In the hospital room. Yes, yes. There were -- there was at least three if not four adults in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that it seemed to you that all these people were relatives of some kind.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- it was the way that they were all seated in the room. There was -- obviously I had interrupted a visit of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as regards your arrival in Ahmic, you said that on the first visit you just passed through and didn't see much, and on the second time you had a specific purpose in mind, to learn facts about it. You went to Upper Ahmici by car; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We went to an upper area of Ahmici, yes. Not in a car but in a tank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a tank. Did you leave the tank in Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the second trip to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the only part that you actually passed through is the area near the road near the mosque, you said that you found some shell casings near two houses near the mosque, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We covered -- we covered, on the second trip -- if you'd like, I could point out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We started in this general area here (indicating). We walked down the road a considerable ways. I don't know exactly how far, but I would imagine it was somewhere around here (indicating). We then entered the vehicles again, continued slightly into this direction, returned, continued up the hill. We went up to an area we could turn around, and I imagine -- okay. We passed this, it became very narrow. There was an area -- it could be this one, it could be this one here, it could be even closer, it could be even this, but there was an area where the vehicles could turn around, and that's about as far as we went. I can't really be sure looking at this, but I would say that we drove -- I can -- without looking at this it's a lot easier. We probably drove about 150 maybe 200 metres past the second mosque when we turned around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, but you said that you did not get off in this area but you passed by the mosque, the lower mosque on the lower part of the road, and that you visited two houses there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I would say it was more than two in the lower part. We certainly went in -- not necessarily into the homes themselves. I don't think we ever went into a house except for just peering inside, or looking through windows and things like that, but we visited a number -- a number of homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were talking about the houses surrounding the lower mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you noticed a lot of damage on those houses, that they had been burnt. You saw bullet marks on some of them, a lot of shell casings around the houses. Does this situation indicate that some kind of combat was taking place there -- had been taking place there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Weapons had been fired. I don't know whose weapons, but weapons were fired obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information provided to you were mostly provided to you by BRITBAT officers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to, as I said, a number of individuals in Zenica, in the cinema, as well as the gentleman in the hospital and members of ECMM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did say that as regards the number of houses that have been destroyed, did you have any information as to how many members of the Croatian armed forces took part in the attack?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: No. We -- we asked that question, and I don't think that anyone could determine that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to the number of victims, according to the estimates at the time, or the findings at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We were told that they -- there was confirmation of 103 killed, and that the Red Cross, or UNHCR or some other body was in the process of putting together a list of names. We sought to get our hands on that list, and I believe we did then or maybe days after when we had arrived back in Zagreb, but we did receive a hand-written list of names. There were 103 names on that list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you talked to in the cinema, were these exclusively women and children or were there men among them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There were also men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there men of military age?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Military age. There were two men that I would say -- I guess military age being from about 18 until 50, I guess, 60, 70, I don't know, but there were two men in their 30's. However, I don't believe that they came from Ahmici. One the men I'm talking about is the individual that produced the key to the room, and the other individual that I talked to was somehow related to someone there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you talked to in the cinema, did they mention that the BH army was in Ahmici or that there had been an armed response on that day, on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: We asked that question and we were told that there was very little resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told how long the conflict in Ahmici lasted? Did they tell you this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think specifically, but that information was available through different stories. I mean, we had a basic idea of the time -- the times that things occurred. Yes. I mean, not specifically, you know, "It started here and ended here," but we had gained that information, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it last approximately, according to the information at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, there was mortar fire or heavy fire that began at approximately 5.30 in the morning, and that it continued with -- other types of fire continued with intensity until about 9.00. I'm just recalling what was told to me and how it was told. There seemed to be a break in the firing around 9.00, but resumed and continued until about midday and about midday it ceased. The reason I can say around midday, is this is when we were told that additional patrols of UNPROFOR had come to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After UNPROFOR left, was there shooting in the village, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I was told, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, were you told which route the people used to flee the village? Did they tell you which way they fled?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: There was a couple of -- I was told of a couple of ways that people escaped. Many -- many stayed in their current hiding places -- or their hiding places until dark. In the case (redacted) actually saved by someone who escorted her to a house. Mr. Ahmic, or [redacted], I believe that he crossed over one of the hills. I really didn't get into those details. There was a number of people that went to the northern part of the village, I believe. There was another group that fled in different directions. There was no one route that was mentioned to me. There were all different stories of how people got out of those situations, and to be quite frank, I didn't really ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to any other village, apart from Ahmici, since this report concerns the wider area, not only Ahmici but some other villages. Did you go to those villages? I'm referring to the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what had happened there? What did you find there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: If that's relevant for this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We received a report, while we were there, from the UNHCR that there was a disturbed population, extremely disturbed population in a village of Miletici, up the hill, and that something had happened there and if we could take a look at it as well, which we agreed. Also, the UNHCR insisted that a British battalion send a patrol there immediately, because there was reports that an atrocity had taken place by an individual, if I recall correctly, who had come down from that village. It was very remote, that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to say that we have got to stop now. So we will continue tomorrow at 9.30. Tomorrow we will go on until 1.00, and then break for lunch from 1.00 to 2.30 and finish at 5.00. So we adjourn now until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
